notes.meaning: God tells Moses to bring Aaron, his two oldest sons, and seventy leaders partway up the mountain. They were to bow down and worship from afar, showing deep reverence before God's holy presence. This special group was chosen to represent the entire nation.

Only Moses is allowed to come near to the Lord, while the other leaders stay back and the rest of the people remain at the foot of the mountain. God sets clear boundaries to show His holiness and how serious it is to approach Him. By standing alone between God and the nation, Moses served as a mediator, pointing ahead to Jesus as the one who brings us to God.

Moses comes down the mountain and shares all of God's rules and commands with the people. The whole congregation answers together, promising to obey everything God has spoken. This united answer showed their willingness to enter into a covenant, which is a sacred, binding agreement with God.

Moses writes down God's laws so the terms of the covenant are permanent and clear to everyone. The next morning, he sets up an altar to represent God and twelve stone pillars to stand for the twelve tribes of Israel. These pillars served as lasting witnesses to the solemn agreement made that day.

Moses sends young, active men to prepare and sacrifice bulls at the altar. Since the regular family of priests had not yet been set apart, these strong young men helped with the heavy work of the offerings. The sacrifices showed total dedication to God and celebrated peaceful fellowship with Him.

Moses divides the blood from the sacrifices into two portions, putting half into basins and splashing the other half against the altar. Splashing blood on the altar showed that God accepted the offering and bound Himself to His promises. The remaining blood was saved to be applied to the people.

Moses reads the newly written book of laws aloud so every person can hear and understand the terms of God's covenant. The people answer a second time, firmly promising not only to listen but to obey. Hearing God's Word clearly is always the foundation for faithful obedience.

Moses sprinkles the remaining blood on the people or their representatives, officially sealing the covenant between God and the nation. This showed that the people were cleansed and joined to God through an atoning sacrifice, an offering that pays for sin and restores peace. Jesus used these very words at the Last Supper when He announced the New Covenant in His own blood.

other.label: Catholic
other.view: The sprinkling of blood at Sinai is seen as a direct pattern for the Eucharist, supporting the teaching that the wine becomes the actual blood of Christ that seals the New Covenant.

notes.meaning: Moses leads Aaron, two of Aaron's sons, and seventy elders up the slopes of Mount Sinai. Because they had just been cleansed by the covenant blood, these leaders were now prepared to climb higher than the rest of the camp. They went up as representatives of the entire nation to meet with God.

The leaders are granted an awesome vision of the God of Israel, gazing in wonder at the radiant pavement beneath His feet. The floor shone like bright blue sapphire stone, clear and brilliant like the open sky. The text focuses only on the dazzling glory under His feet to remind us of His majesty.

other.label: Modern scholarship
other.view: Some scholars suggest the leaders did not see a bodily shape, but only the brilliant pavement where God stood as they bowed face-down in worship.

notes.meaning: Although people feared that seeing God would bring instant death, God did not harm these leaders. Instead, they ate and drank their peace offerings in His presence, celebrating their new relationship with Him. Sharing this meal was a comforting sign of peace and fellowship with the Lord.

God calls Moses to leave the elders and climb to the top of the mountain for a lengthy stay. There God promises to hand him stone tablets containing the Ten Commandments, written by God Himself. Having the laws engraved on stone showed that God's moral commands are permanent and must be taught to future generations.

Moses begins his climb, taking his faithful helper Joshua along with him part of the way. Joshua was being trained in close fellowship with God so that he would be ready to lead Israel in the future. Moses then continued higher toward the place where God called him.

Before climbing higher, Moses instructs the elders to wait and leaves Aaron and Hur in charge of the camp. If any legal disagreements arose among the people, these two trusted men were given authority to settle them. Moses made careful plans so the community would stay orderly and peaceful while he was away.

Moses ascends higher, and a thick cloud covers the mountain. This cloud was a visible sign of God's presence, revealing that God was there while shielding His full glory from human eyes. It showed that God is near to His people yet far beyond human understanding.

God's glorious presence rests upon Mount Sinai, keeping the mountain covered in the cloud for six full days. Moses waited patiently during this time, preparing his heart before God spoke to him out of the cloud on the seventh day. Taking time to wait on God prepares us to hear His voice clearly.

To the people watching from the camp below, the glory of the Lord looked like a blazing, devouring fire on the mountaintop. This fiery sight reminded Israel of God's awesome power, holiness, and justice. It called the whole nation to worship Him with deep reverence and awe.

Moses enters right into the cloud where God's presence dwells, sustained entirely by God without food or water. He stays on the mountain for forty days and forty nights to receive God's laws and the plans for the tabernacle. God gave Moses supernatural strength to spend this extended time in His presence.
